2.3 — Healing Pickups & the Max-Health Cap

You can gain wealth and lose health. Now you need a way to get health back — and the moment you add healing, you create a new kind of problem. Healing without a limit is not a feature, it is an exploit. Today you compare the potion against both things you have already built, then discover that a value with a ceiling needs a rule, not just arithmetic.

Comparative Thinking ~15 min

Good engineers do not design from nothing. When you meet a new mechanic, ask what you have already built that behaves like it:

ComparisonAnalysis
How is the potion like the coin? Both are pickups: trigger colliders, handled by OnTriggerEnter2D, and destroyed on contact so they cannot be taken twice. Almost all of your coin code is reusable.
How is the potion like the spike? Both change health — and health lives on PlayerController, exactly where your coin count lives.
How is the potion different from both? It raises a value that now has a ceiling. Without a rule, ten potions means ten times the health, and the game stops being a game.
There is no potion art in this project — you are going to make one. There is no Potion prefab, no Potion tag, and no potion sprite in Assets/Artwork. So: pick a sprite you do have, and tint it with the Sprite Renderer's Color field so it cannot be mistaken for a coin. Create the tag yourself. Building a mechanic with borrowed art is called greyboxing, and it is what professionals do all day — the mechanic is the work; the art is a placeholder until someone draws the real thing.

Socratic: Similar, Different, and Why It Matters

  1. The potion reuses the coin's trigger, its callback, and its destroy. What is the only thing that genuinely differs?
  2. Without a ceiling, a player who collects ten potions has ten times the health. Which breaks first — the challenge, the economy, or the feedback the player gets?
  3. The rule "health must never exceed the maximum" has to live somewhere. Name two places it could live, and say which one keeps the rule true no matter which script calls the healing method.
  4. If a second healing source arrives in Unit 5 — a heart, a shrine, a level-up — is a ceiling check inside the potion script still enough? What does your answer say about where rules belong?
Read Function-Level Examples ~15 min

Four ways to keep a number inside its limits, each from a different system. Read them in isolation and work out what each one can and cannot do:

Example 1 — A water reservoir dam, using if:

if (currentGallons > maxReservoirCapacity)
{
    currentGallons = maxReservoirCapacity;
}

Example 2 — An electric scooter battery, using Mathf.Min:

// Mathf.Min returns the smaller of the two, so the battery cannot charge past 100%
batteryLevel = Mathf.Min(batteryLevel + chargeAdded, 100f);

Example 3 — A spaceship thruster, using Mathf.Clamp:

// Mathf.Clamp bounds a value at BOTH ends at once - here, 0 and 100
thrusterPower = Mathf.Clamp(requestedThrust, 0, 100);

Example 4 — A reservoir overflow alarm, an if with a side effect:

if (currentGallons >= maxReservoirCapacity)
{
    Debug.Log("Overflow: intake refused.");
}

Predict Before Building

  1. currentGallons is 95 and 20 gallons arrive. Trace Example 1: what is the value before the check, inside the body, and after it?
  2. What is the difference between Mathf.Min and Mathf.Clamp? In a game where damage can drive health down as well as up, which one covers both ends?
  3. Example 4 logs a refusal. Which of the first three examples could produce that message on its own — and why can the other two not?
  4. If you clamp health at 0, have you also implemented death? What is the difference between "this value cannot go below zero" and "the player dies"?
Build Lab: The Potion ~25 min
Architectural specification: the prefab.
  • In the Hierarchy, right-click → 2D Object → Sprite. Name it Potion, then drag it into Assets/Prefabs so it becomes reusable. What is the difference between the object in the scene and the asset in the folder?
  • Which sprite will you use, and what Color tint makes it obviously not a coin at a glance?
  • Add a collider. Trigger or solid — and what is your reason? Which of the two things you built this unit does this make it most like?
  • You are about to create a tag that does not exist in this project. Where does the tag list actually live? Does the prefab need the tag, or does one instance in the scene?
  • Before you write CompareTag("Potion") in code, how do you check the tag exists? What happens if you get the spelling wrong?
Architectural specification: the rule.
  • What field holds the maximum health? How is it different from the current-health field, and which of the two should be the designer's tuning knob?
  • Where exactly does the ceiling get applied — before the heal, after the heal, or inside the method that changes health? Which of those cannot be bypassed by a future caller?
  • Pick one of the three capping approaches from the examples. What does your choice do that the other two cannot?
  • If you chose Mathf.Clamp, what is the lower bound — and what does clamping at 0 mean for the death check you wrote in 2.2?
Architectural specification: the trigger.
  • Which callback, and which tag check?
  • Which method on the player do you call, and do you pass a positive or a negative number?
  • Do you destroy the potion? Which object — other.gameObject or gameObject?
  • What should happen when a player already at full health touches a potion: consume it, or leave it on the ground? Both are defensible. Pick one, and name the extra check your choice requires and where that check belongs.

Save, press Play, and verify. Drop your health on a spike, then walk into a potion and confirm it comes back up. Then walk into another potion at full health and confirm your rule holds.

Bug Hunt: Boundary Conditions ~15 min

Bug Hunt

  1. Set maximum health to 5 in the Inspector. Does the code still cap correctly, or did you hardcode 3 somewhere in your file?
  2. Change your cap comparison from > to >=, or the reverse. With health exactly at the maximum, what happens now — and how would you ever have noticed if you only ever tested from the middle?
  3. Forget to create the tag, then call CompareTag("Potion") anyway. What does Unity report? Why is a loud error better here than silence?
  4. Make the potion solid instead of a trigger. What does the player do when they walk into it, and does the heal still fire?
  5. Heal at full health under each of the three capping approaches. Which one silently does nothing, and which one could tell you the heal was wasted?
  6. Set maximum health below your current health while the game is running. What does your rule do — and is that a bug or a feature?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Testing Mathf.Clamp

  1. Rewrite your ceiling using Mathf.Clamp(health, 0, maxHealth). Test both spikes and potions. Does one line replace two separate checks — and what did you have to be careful about?
  2. Implement your answer to "should a full-health player waste a potion?" Which check did you add, and where did you put it?
  3. Read the docs for Mathf.Min and Mathf.Clamp. Which would you use if a designer said "health may go negative — that is how we count overkill damage"?
  4. Where else in this game will a value need a ceiling — a fire rate, a detection radius, a jump count, a coin total? Which of the three approaches would you reach for there, and is it the same one you chose here?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain how the potion is like the coin, like the spike, and unlike both
  • Create a prefab and a brand-new project tag from scratch
  • Explain the overheal exploit, and which selection rule prevents it
  • Compare if, Mathf.Min and Mathf.Clamp, and defend the one you chose
  • Explain why the rule lives in the method that changes health rather than in the potion
  • Test at the boundary — health exactly at maximum — instead of only in the middle
  • Commit and push
